voiceInstructions: Warm, engaging female teacher with a natural General American English accent. Relaxed, welcoming and lightly playful, with a gentle smile and conversational rhythm. Keep scientific terms precise and avoid an announcer cadence. Slow down for equations, numbers and conversions. Give brief natural thinking pauses after questions. Do not add words or laughter absent from the script.
title: Nuclei, binding energy, fission and fusion

sources.title: NTA: Official JEE Main 2026 syllabus, Physics Unit 18

chapters.title: Count the particles before using the mass
chapters.formula: A = Z + N; one u = 1/12 of a neutral carbon-12 atom's mass
points: Z counts protons; N counts neutrons; A counts nucleons.
Isotopes have the same Z but different neutron counts.
Mass number is an integer count, not the exact mass in u.
chapters.script: Hey, welcome back. Today we look inside the nucleus and connect its structure with energy. Start with three symbols. Z is the number of protons, N is the number of neutrons, and A is the total number of nucleons. Therefore A equals Z plus N. For iron fifty-six, Z is twenty-six. Subtract twenty-six from fifty-six and you get thirty neutrons. A neutral atom also has twenty-six electrons, but those electrons are not included in the nuclear mass number. Isotopes have the same proton number and different neutron numbers. Their chemistry can be similar because they belong to the same element, while their nuclear properties can differ. Now a units trap. Mass number fifty-six does not mean the actual atomic mass is exactly fifty-six unified atomic mass units. A is a count. The unit u is defined as one twelfth of the mass of a neutral carbon-twelve atom in its ground state at rest. Notice the word atom, not bare nucleus. Atomic mass tables generally include the electrons of neutral atoms. Nuclear mass tables do not. We will keep that distinction when calculating binding energy. Pause and test the notation: if an isotope has A equal to forty and Z equal to twenty, how many neutrons are inside? Twenty. Begin each nuclear question by counting particles and identifying whether the stated mass belongs to a nucleus or an atom. That small check saves a surprising number of mistakes.

chapters.title: Nuclear size and nearly constant density
chapters.formula: R approximately R0 A^(1/3), with R0 approximately 1.2 fm
points: Nuclear volume grows roughly in proportion to A.
The relation is an empirical average, not an exact sharp boundary.
chapters.script: A nucleus is incredibly small compared with an atom. A useful empirical estimate for its radius is R zero times A to the one-third power. Use R zero approximately one point two femtometers for our examples. A femtometer is ten to the minus fifteen meters. The one-third power means a cube root. Why that particular dependence? Nuclear matter has approximately the same density across many nuclei. Adding nucleons roughly adds volume. If volume grows in proportion to A and a sphere's volume grows as radius cubed, radius must grow as the cube root of A. Real nuclei have diffuse boundaries and can be nonspherical, so this is an average model rather than an exact ruler for every isotope. Take A equal to one hundred twenty-five. The cube root is five, giving radius about six femtometers. Now compare nuclei with mass numbers sixty-four and two hundred sixteen. Their cube roots are four and six. The radius ratio is six over four, or one point five. The mass-number ratio is larger, three point three seven five. Their volumes have approximately that same larger ratio, because volume depends on radius cubed. Think before answering a ratio question: does it ask for radius, volume, or density? They are not interchangeable. In the simple spherical model, mass and volume both scale with A, so A cancels from the density expression. Nearly constant nuclear density follows from the same scaling assumption; it is not an independent numerical coincidence.

chapters.title: Mass defect measures binding energy
chapters.formula: Using atomic masses: Delta m = Z mH + N mn - Matom; B = Delta m c^2
points: Bound systems have lower rest mass than their separated constituents.
With neutral atomic masses, use hydrogen-atom mass consistently.
1 u c^2 approximately 931.5 MeV; deuterium B approximately 2.224 MeV.
chapters.script: Here comes the central energy idea. A bound nucleus has a lower rest mass than its separated protons and neutrons. That difference is called the mass defect. Energy is released when the bound state forms, and energy must be supplied to separate it completely. This does not violate conservation: total mass-energy, including released radiation and kinetic energy, is conserved. If you use bare nuclear masses, subtract the nuclear mass from the sum of bare proton and neutron masses. If you use neutral atomic masses instead, use hydrogen-atom mass for each proton contribution. The electron rest masses then cancel to excellent approximation, while small electronic binding corrections are neglected at this nuclear scale. Let's calculate for deuterium, containing one proton and one neutron. Use hydrogen-atom mass one point zero zero seven eight two five u, neutron mass one point zero zero eight six six five u, and deuterium atomic mass two point zero one four one zero two u. Add the first two and subtract the third. The defect is zero point zero zero two three eight eight u. Multiply by nine hundred thirty-one point five mega electron volts per u. The binding energy is approximately two point two two four mega electron volts. For binding energy per nucleon, divide by A equal to two, giving about one point one one two mega electron volts. Do not mix a bare proton mass with a neutral deuterium atomic mass. Consistent mass bookkeeping comes before the multiplication.

chapters.title: Read the binding-energy curve carefully
chapters.formula: Binding energy per nucleon = B/A; reaction energy depends on total B
points: The curve reaches roughly 8.8 MeV per nucleon near iron and nickel.
Heavy and very light nuclei generally lie below this peak.
Use total binding energies or rest masses for an exact reaction Q.
chapters.script: Now plot binding energy per nucleon against mass number. For very light nuclei the values are relatively small, with important irregularities between neighboring nuclei. The broad curve rises toward a peak near the iron and nickel region, around eight point eight mega electron volts per nucleon, and then declines gradually for very heavy nuclei. This graph gives an energy direction, not a universal rule that every imaginable reaction must occur. Light nuclei can release energy by combining into products with greater total binding. Some heavy nuclei can release energy by splitting into more tightly bound products. Here is the reason: greater binding means a lower combined rest mass for the same conserved particles, with the difference available as released energy. Be careful with the word per. To calculate the exact energy of a reaction, compare total binding energies or consistent total rest masses of all reactants and products. A single per-nucleon number cannot replace that bookkeeping. If a nucleus with A equal to fifty has binding energy per nucleon eight mega electron volts, its total binding energy is four hundred mega electron volts. Pause before using that total as reaction energy. It is not automatically the energy released in any particular change. The products also carry binding energy. Likewise, a large binding energy per nucleon does not by itself prove that every possible radioactive decay is forbidden. Charge, nucleon balance, available final states, and the complete energy comparison matter. Read the curve as a useful trend, then calculate the stated reaction.

chapters.title: Fission, fusion and the reaction energy
chapters.formula: Q = (sum initial rest masses - sum final rest masses)c^2
points: One possible channel: U-235 + n -> Ba-141 + Kr-92 + 3n.
Fusion illustration: D + T -> He-4 + n, releasing about 17.6 MeV.
Balance mass number and charge; count every product's mass.
chapters.script: Let's bring the energy story together. Fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into lighter products. One possible illustrative channel is uranium two hundred thirty-five plus a neutron forming barium one hundred forty-one, krypton ninety-two, and three neutrons. Count the mass numbers: two hundred thirty-six on the left, and one hundred forty-one plus ninety-two plus three on the right. Charge numbers also balance: ninety-two equals fifty-six plus thirty-six. Real fission has many product channels, so this example is not the only outcome. Energy release is typically of order two hundred mega electron volts per fission, depending on the complete channel and energy accounting. Fusion combines light nuclei. An illustrative reaction is deuterium plus tritium forming helium four and a neutron. Mass number is five on both sides, and charge number is two on both sides. This reaction releases about seventeen point six mega electron volts. The positive nuclei repel electrically, so merely having an energy-favorable product does not remove the approach barrier; quantum tunneling also matters. Our focus is conceptual nuclear energy, not engineering a device. For a numerical example, if the total initial rest mass exceeds the final total by zero point zero one eight nine u, Q is that difference times nine hundred thirty-one point five, approximately seventeen point six mega electron volts. A positive Q means energy is released. A negative Q means energy must be supplied, with additional kinematic conditions potentially relevant. Balance particles first, use one consistent mass convention, and only then evaluate the energy difference.
